steps.title: Both have a right to the ball
steps.body: Once a forward pass is in the air, the receiver and the defender both have a right to play the ball. Neither may push, grab or cut off the other to stop a catch. After any foul, the referee gives the hand signal and announces the foul and the player's number.

steps.title: Defensive pass interference
steps.body: In the NFL it is a spot foul: the offense gets the ball where the foul happened, with an automatic first down. In the end zone, the ball goes to the 1-yard line.

steps.title: Offensive pass interference
steps.body: A receiver who pushes off to create space is called for offensive pass interference: 10 yards.

steps.title: Illegal contact
steps.body: Before the pass is thrown, a defender may jam a receiver within 5 yards of the line. Contact beyond 5 yards is illegal contact: 5 yards and an automatic first down.

steps.prompt: A defender grabs a receiver's arm 30 yards downfield as the ball arrives. Where does the NFL spot the ball?
choices: At the spot of the foul
steps.explanation: Defensive pass interference is a spot foul in the NFL, plus an automatic first down.

steps.statement: In the NFL, a cornerback may jam a receiver 10 yards downfield before the pass is thrown.
steps.explanation: NFL defenders may contact a receiver only within 5 yards of the line. Past that, before the throw, it's illegal contact: 5 yards and an automatic first down.

steps.prompt: A receiver shoves the defender away just before the catch. What is called?
steps.explanation: Pushing off to create separation is offensive pass interference: 10 yards.

steps.prompt: How many yards is offensive holding?
steps.explanation: 10 yards. Defensive holding is 5 yards plus an automatic first down.

steps.prompt: After a foul, how does the referee tell everyone what was called?
choices: A hand signal and an announcement
A whistle and a flag at the spot
A note to the head coach
steps.explanation: Every foul has its own hand signal, and the referee announces the foul and the player's number.

steps.title: Roughing the passer
steps.body: Hitting the quarterback after he has thrown, hitting his head or neck, or landing on him with full body weight: 15 yards and an automatic first down.

steps.title: Unnecessary roughness
steps.body: Extra hits away from the play, late hits on a runner who is down or out of bounds: 15 yards.

steps.title: Targeting is not an NFL foul
steps.body: "Targeting" is a college and high school rule: forcible contact to the head or neck, or with the crown of the helmet. In college it means 15 yards and an ejection. The NFL penalizes helmet hits under its own rules instead.

steps.prompt: A defender hits the quarterback two steps after the ball is gone. What is the penalty?
steps.explanation: A late hit on a quarterback who has thrown is roughing the passer: 15 yards and a first down.

steps.statement: In college football, a targeting foul also ejects the player.
steps.explanation: Targeting is 15 yards plus an ejection after review.

steps.prompt: Match each foul to its usual NFL yardage.
steps.explanation: The most dangerous fouls carry the biggest penalties.

steps.prompt: After the whistle, a defender shoves a ball carrier who is already out of bounds. What is the call?
steps.explanation: Late or extra hits are unnecessary roughness: 15 yards.

lessons.title: Replay, Challenges and Overtime
lessons.blurb: How calls get fixed, and how ties end.

steps.title: Coach's challenge
steps.body: An NFL coach throws a red flag to challenge a call. Each team gets two challenges, and a third if both succeed. A lost challenge costs a timeout.

steps.title: Automatic reviews
steps.body: Scoring plays and turnovers are reviewed by the replay official without a challenge. Inside the last two minutes of each half and in overtime, reviews start from the replay booth, not a coach's flag.

steps.title: Overtime (as of the 2025 season)
steps.body: In the NFL regular season, overtime is one 10-minute period, and both teams get a possession unless the defense scores on the first one. After that, the next score wins. A regular-season game can end in a tie.

steps.prompt: A coach's challenge fails. What does it cost?
steps.explanation: A lost challenge costs a timeout, so a coach needs one left to challenge.

steps.statement: A coach must throw the red flag to get a touchdown reviewed.
steps.explanation: Scoring plays are reviewed automatically by the replay official.

steps.prompt: With 1:30 left in the half, a coach wants a sideline catch reviewed. What happens?
choices: The replay official decides; coaches can't challenge
The coach throws the red flag to challenge
Nothing: catches can't be reviewed now
Both coaches must agree to a review
steps.explanation: Inside two minutes of each half, reviews come from the replay booth, not the coach.

steps.prompt: NFL regular season: the team that gets the ball first in overtime kicks a field goal. What happens?
choices: The other team gets a possession
Sudden death from the next play
The game ends in a tie
steps.explanation: Both teams get a possession unless the defense scores on the first one. After that, the next score wins.
